metadata.title: Glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies in stiff-man syndrome and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus exhibit similarities and differences in epitope recognition.
metadata.abstract: Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) is an autoantigen in two autoimmune diseases, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM) and stiff-man syndrome (SMS). However, most individuals with one of these diseases do not have the other disease. Prior studies have suggested that the natures of the GAD Abs associated with each of these diseases are different, which may have implications for the autoimmune pathogenesis. We have compared the GAD autoantibody profile and have mapped GAD protein epitope regions in the two diseases using an immunoprecipitation assay with recombinant GAD 65 and GAD 67 proteins, GAD protein fragments, and synthetic GAD peptides, as well as chimeric GAD proteins. Our results indicate that individuals with SMS have GAD Abs in 100- to 500-fold higher titer than individuals with IDDM. The population of GAD Abs in SMS sera is quite complex and includes those that recognize at least three GAD 65 epitope regions located between amino acids 1-16, 188-442, and 442-563. These types of GAD Abs are not found in IDDM sera. All SMS sera also had Ab specificity that binds GAD 67 in a region highly homologous to amino acids 188-442 of GAD 65. In contrast to prior studies that used immunoblotting to measure GAD Abs, we find GAD Abs in SMS sera also target two conformation-dependent regions of GAD 65, one located in the middle and one near the C-terminus of the protein. These two regions of the GAD 65 protein are similar to regions targeted by GAD 65-specific Abs found in individuals with IDDM. These results indicate that although disease-specific epitopes may exist, there is also overlap in the humoral response between the two diseases.

converts glutamic acid to the neurotransmitter y-aminobutyric acid 
(GABA), is found in the cytoplasm and microsecretory vesicles of 
GABA-secreting neurons and pancreatic cells (4, 5). GAD exists 
as two protein isoforms of 65 kDa (585 amino acids) and 67 kDa 
(594 amino acids), which are encoded by two distinct genes (6).

tein, but differ substantially in the N-terminal region. Differences 
in the N-terminus of the protein are responsible for targeting GAD 
65 and GAD 67 to different intracellular locations (7). In contrast 
to rat pancreatic islets that express both GAD 65 and GAD 67, 
human pancreatic islets contain only GAD  65 (8, 9). 
GAD autoantibodies were initially discovered in individuals 
with SMS (3). Subsequent studies by Baekkeskov et al. demon- 
strated that GAD autoantibodies are also found in individuals with 
IDDM (1 0). GAD autoantibodies are an important marker of the 
autoimmune process of IDDM since they are present in the vast 
majority of individuals with new-onset diabetes as well as in many 
individuals in the prediabetic stage of the disease (I 1-13). The 
possible role of GAD as the primary autoantigen in IDDM has 
been suggested by recent demonstrations of cellular autoimmunity 
directed at GAD in IDDM (14, 15) as well as autoimmunity di- 
rected at GAD in an animal model of IDDM (16, 17). 
Although GAD Abs are found in both SMS and IDDM, the 
GAD autoantibody profile in the two diseases differs. For example, 
GAD Abs in SMS bind denatured GAD protein utilized in immu- 
noblotting while the GAD autoantibodies in IDDM do not bind the 
protein under such conditions (IO). In addition, co-incubation of 
purified GAD protein and SMS sera inhibits the enzymatic activity 
of GAD, which suggests that these GAD Abs from SMS bind the 
active site of the enzyme (18). This inhibition does not occur with 
GAD Abs from IDDM. 
Other studies of the GAD Abs in the two diseases have focused 
on the GAD protein epitopes at which the autoantibodies are di- 
rected. Utilizing immunoblotting of recombinant GAD protein, 
Butler et al. mapped the major GAD 65 epitope in a large number 
of individuals with SMS to the COOH terminus of the protein 
(amino  acids 475-484 and amino acids 571-585) (19). Li et al. 
also used immunoblotting to detect reactivity of SMS sera to two

synthetic GAD peptides (amino acids 354-368 and amino acids 
390-402) which are thought to span the active site of the GAD 
enzyme (20). Kim et al. recently reported that SMS sera have 
higher GAD autoantibody levels than IDDM sera and target a con- 
tinuous protein epitope located in the first eight amino acids of 
GAD 65 (21). The N-terminal epitope was not bound by IDDM 
sera. These results suggest that SMS sera have GAD Abs that bind 
linear protein epitopes. 
Conversely, GAD Abs in IDDM do not bind denatured GAD 
protein, GAD fragments, or GAD peptides, which implies that 
these GAD Abs bind an epitope dependent on protein conforma- 
tion (10, 22, 23). This concept has led to the suggestion that GAD 
Abs in SMS and in IDDM differ in their epitope recognition pat- 
tern  and that disease-specific epitopes may exist (1 8, 19, 21). How- 
ever,  a limitation of prior reports is that studies with SMS sera 
were optimized for detecting Abs that bind linear epitopes (immu- 
noblotting), while studies in IDDM used immunoprecipitation of 
nondenatured GAD protein as the assay system. Because of these 
experimental differences, the results of epitope mapping are diffi- 
cult to compare. To compare the GAD Abs in the two diseases and 
to determine if disease-specific GAD epitopes exist, we have 
mapped the protein epitope regions in sera from individuals with 
SMS and individuals with IDDM in an immunoprecipitation assay 
using recombinant GAD 65 and GAD 67 proteins, GAD protein 
fragments, GAD peptides, and chimeric GAD proteins. 
Materials and Methods 
Preparation of GAD protein 
Full length rat GAD  65 and human GAD  67 cDNAs were transcribed into 
GAD RNA using T7 RNA Polymerase in an in vitro transcription system 
(Megascript, Ambion, Austin, TX) (23). Metabolically labeled, recombi- 
nant rat GAD 65 and human GAD 67 proteins were prepared by in vitro 
translation of GAD RNA with reticulocyte lysate (Promega, Madison,WI) 
using an amino acid mixture containing ["Slmethionine (1 200 Ci/mmol) 
(23).  TCA precipitation of the translation products was utilized to deter- 
mine the percentage of incorporation of the labeled amino acid in the GAD 
protein. Percentage of incorporation was calculated as (radioactivity in 
TCA-precipitated proteidtotal radioactivity in the reaction) X 100 and 
ranged from 20 to  60%.  The rat GAD 65 protein reacted with a widely used 
sheep polyclonal GAD antiserum and two mAbs, GAD 1 and GAD 6  (24, 
25).  The polyclonal GAD antiserum was a gift of  Dr. Enrico Mugnaini 
(University of Connecticut, Hartford, CT) and Virginia Weise (Laboratory 
of Clinical Science at the National Institute of Mental Health, Bethesda, 
MD) and reacted with both GAD  65 and GAD 67. The GAD 1 mAb was 
a gift of Dr. David Gottlieb (Washington University, Washington, MO); 
the GAD  6 mAb was obtained from the Developmental Studies Hybridoma 
Bank at the University of Iowa, Ames, 1A (National Institute of Child 
Development Contract No. I-HD-2-3144). As shown by other groups, the 
GAD  6 mAb reacted only with the GAD 65 isoform (9. 19, 21, 26, 27). 
GAD 65 protein fragments containing amino acids 1-195  and  1-360 
were prepared from restriction enzyme fragments of GAD  65 cDNA after 
linearization with HinclI and NsiI enzymes, respectively. PCR was utilized 
to create GAD 65 cDNA fragments encoding amino acids 188-585 and 
444-585 (23). Each primer used was complementary to published GAD 
cDNA sequence with incorporation of a unique restriction enzyme site to 
facilitate subcloning. The PCR products were either purified using a Gene- 
clean I1 kit (Bio 101, Vista, CA) after restriction enzyme digestion or 
directly subcloned into pT7 Blue plasmid (Novagen, Madison, WI). The 
GAD 65 cDNA fragment encoding amino acids 188-585 was digested 
with Stul to create a cDNA fragment encoding amino acids 188-442. A 
GAD 65 cDNA fragment encoding amino acids 361-585 was created with 
a unique BglII site in the GAD  65  cDNA. Fragments of the GAD 65 protein 
were then prepared from the cDNA fragments by  in vitro transcription and 
translation as described above. Since there are 30 pmol of hot ["Slmethi- 
onine and 175 pmol  of unlabeled methionine in the translation reaction, 
approximately one in  six to seven methionines will be labeled (28). Since 
incorporation of [3sSJmethionine will be a random event. the number of 
methionine residues in a protein fragment was linearly related to the 
amount of label incorporated (R2 = 0.99).  Thus, the specific activity of a 
GAD protein is a function of the number of methionine residues in that 
protein. 
Serum samples 
Serum samples were collected from individuals with new-onset diabetes 
(n = 30) as well as from control (nondiabetic) individuals and stored at 
-20°C.  The clinical features of these sera have been previously described 
(23). Serum samples from individuals with the clinical diagnosis of stiff- 
man syndrome (n = 5) were obtained from Dr. Vanda Lennon, Mayo 
Clinic, Rochester, MN; from Dr. Robert Schmidli, Royal Melbourne Hos- 
pital, Melbourne, Australia; and from Drs. Roberto Gianani and George 
Eisenbarth, Barbara Davis Center of Childhood Diabetes, Denver, CO. 
SMS serum 3 (as noted in figures) was utilized as the standard serum in 
both international GAD autoantibody comparisons sponsored by the Im- 
munology of Diabetes Workshop (29).  Two of the individuals with SMS 
also have diabetes (SMS 3  and  4). 
Immunoprecipitation of GAD protein 
A total of 15 yl of diluted serum (diluted 1/10 to 1/50,000) from individ- 
uals with stiff-man syndrome, new-onset IDDM, or from control subjects 
was incubated with 30 yl of metabolically-labeled GAD protein for 12 to 
15 h at 4°C in a total assay volume of 60 pI (23). Based on percent 
incorporation rate of [3sS]methionine, 50,000 cpm of each GAD protein 
were used  in each assay tube. All dilutions of serum and GAD protein were 
made with Tris-buffered saline/0.05% Tween 20 (TBST). Protein A-Sepha- 
rose (PAS, Sigma Chemical Co., St. Louis, MO) was washed and resus- 
pended in TBST to a 2% solution. Six microliters of PAS (final  bed vol- 
ume) were added to the reaction and mixed for 1 h  at 4°C with gentle 
rotation. Using this volume of PAS, protein A is  in excess of  Ig  in the 
serum (manufacturer's specification). We confirmed experimentally that 6 
yl of PAS quantitatively immunoprecipitates Igs from the serum samples. 
The protein A-Sepharose pellets were washed three times with 500 pl of 
TBST and resuspended in 100 yl of 1% SDS and counted by p scintillation 
counting. All samples were assayed in duplicates. The relative amount of 
GAD protein immunoprecipitated was expressed as a molar ratio ((cpm of 
GAD protein immunoprecipitated by test serum minus cpm  of GAD pro- 
tein immunoprecipitated by normal serum)/(number of methionine residues 
in the GAD protein fragment)) as previously described (23). In  an inter- 
laboratory comparison of GAD Ab assays (29), this assay was positive in 
82% of sera from individuals with new-onset diabetes, 100% of bera from 
individuals with prediabetes, and 3% of normal individuals (1994 Work- 
shop results). Whether SMS or IDDM sera reacted with a particular GAD 
fragment was determined by assaying normal sera in parallel and from 
standards established during our laboratory's participation in international 
GAD Ab workshops (29, 30). A serum was determined to be positive for 
a particular GAD fragment if its reactivity exceeded the reactivity of five 
normal sera with that GAD fragment. 
Blocking of Ab  binding to GAD protein 
Unlabeled, full length GAD  65,  GAD 67, and GAD protein fragments were 
prepared in the reticulocyte lysate system as detailed above except that the 
amino acid mixture contained only unlabeled methionine. Since the me- 
thionine concentration in the reticulocyte lysate system is not limiting, 
similar amounts of cold and labeled protein were synthesized in a trans- 
lation reaction, diluted to the desired molar ratios, and then used for com- 
petition studies. For competition experiments. a dilution curve of a partic- 
ular serum was used to select the serum dilution in which binding to the 
GAD protein was easily detectable but less than maximum. Both labeled 
and unlabeled translation reactions were diluted five to eightfold so that the 
molar ratio of labeled protein to cold protein was 1 :3 to 1 :6.  The molar ratio 
was the same for different protein fragments. For the blocking studies, 
unlabeled GAD protein or reticulocyte lysate without GAD protein (neg- 
ative control) was incubated with a dilution of the test serum for 3 h at 
room temperature; this mixture was then added to 50,000 cpm of 
["SICAD protein and incubated for 12 to 15 h at 4°C (23). Each serum 
used in the blocking studies was diluted according to a previously per- 
formed serum dilution curve to allow for detection of Ab activity and to 
insure that the blocking assay was performed under the condition of Ag 
excess (serum dilutions ranged from 1/100 to 1/1000). PAS was added and 
immunoprecipitation was performed as described above. The immunopre- 
cipitate was analyzed by scintillation counting and expressed as the per- 
centage of inhibition of GAD binding following preincubation with reticu- 
locyte lysate without GAD protein. 
Synthesis of GAD peptides 
Synthetic  GAD  65  peptides  (20  amino  acids in length)  were  synthesized 
as previously  described (16) and  had a purity  greater than 85% by mass 
spectroscopy.

nondenatured GAD protein as the assay system. Because of these 
experimental differences, the results of epitope mapping are diffi- 
cult to compare. To compare the GAD Abs in the two diseases and 
to determine if disease-specific GAD epitopes exist, we have 
mapped the protein epitope regions in sera from individuals with 
SMS and individuals with IDDM in an immunoprecipitation assay 
using recombinant GAD 65 and GAD 67 proteins, GAD protein 
fragments, GAD peptides, and chimeric GAD proteins. 
Materials and Methods 
Preparation of GAD protein 
Full length rat GAD  65 and human GAD  67 cDNAs were transcribed into 
GAD RNA using T7 RNA Polymerase in an in vitro transcription system 
(Megascript, Ambion, Austin, TX) (23). Metabolically labeled, recombi- 
nant rat GAD 65 and human GAD 67 proteins were prepared by in vitro 
translation of GAD RNA with reticulocyte lysate (Promega, Madison,WI) 
using an amino acid mixture containing ["Slmethionine (1 200 Ci/mmol) 
(23).  TCA precipitation of the translation products was utilized to deter- 
mine the percentage of incorporation of the labeled amino acid in the GAD 
protein. Percentage of incorporation was calculated as (radioactivity in 
TCA-precipitated proteidtotal radioactivity in the reaction) X 100 and 
ranged from 20 to  60%.  The rat GAD 65 protein reacted with a widely used 
sheep polyclonal GAD antiserum and two mAbs, GAD 1 and GAD 6  (24, 
25).  The polyclonal GAD antiserum was a gift of  Dr. Enrico Mugnaini 
(University of Connecticut, Hartford, CT) and Virginia Weise (Laboratory 
of Clinical Science at the National Institute of Mental Health, Bethesda, 
MD) and reacted with both GAD  65 and GAD 67. The GAD 1 mAb was 
a gift of Dr. David Gottlieb (Washington University, Washington, MO); 
the GAD  6 mAb was obtained from the Developmental Studies Hybridoma 
Bank at the University of Iowa, Ames, 1A (National Institute of Child 
Development Contract No. I-HD-2-3144). As shown by other groups, the 
GAD  6 mAb reacted only with the GAD 65 isoform (9. 19, 21, 26, 27). 
GAD 65 protein fragments containing amino acids 1-195  and  1-360 
were prepared from restriction enzyme fragments of GAD  65 cDNA after 
linearization with HinclI and NsiI enzymes, respectively. PCR was utilized 
to create GAD 65 cDNA fragments encoding amino acids 188-585 and 
444-585 (23). Each primer used was complementary to published GAD 
cDNA sequence with incorporation of a unique restriction enzyme site to 
facilitate subcloning. The PCR products were either purified using a Gene- 
clean I1 kit (Bio 101, Vista, CA) after restriction enzyme digestion or 
directly subcloned into pT7 Blue plasmid (Novagen, Madison, WI). The 
GAD 65 cDNA fragment encoding amino acids 188-585 was digested 
with Stul to create a cDNA fragment encoding amino acids 188-442. A 
GAD 65 cDNA fragment encoding amino acids 361-585 was created with 
a unique BglII site in the GAD  65  cDNA. Fragments of the GAD 65 protein 
were then prepared from the cDNA fragments by  in vitro transcription and 
translation as described above. Since there are 30 pmol of hot ["Slmethi- 
onine and 175 pmol  of unlabeled methionine in the translation reaction, 
approximately one in  six to seven methionines will be labeled (28). Since 
incorporation of [3sSJmethionine will be a random event. the number of 
methionine residues in a protein fragment was linearly related to the 
amount of label incorporated (R2 = 0.99).  Thus, the specific activity of a 
GAD protein is a function of the number of methionine residues in that 
protein. 
Serum samples 
Serum samples were collected from individuals with new-onset diabetes 
(n = 30) as well as from control (nondiabetic) individuals and stored at 
-20°C.  The clinical features of these sera have been previously described 
(23). Serum samples from individuals with the clinical diagnosis of stiff- 
man syndrome (n = 5) were obtained from Dr. Vanda Lennon, Mayo 
Clinic, Rochester, MN; from Dr. Robert Schmidli, Royal Melbourne Hos- 
pital, Melbourne, Australia; and from Drs. Roberto Gianani and George 
Eisenbarth, Barbara Davis Center of Childhood Diabetes, Denver, CO. 
SMS serum 3 (as noted in figures) was utilized as the standard serum in 
both international GAD autoantibody comparisons sponsored by the Im- 
munology of Diabetes Workshop (29).  Two of the individuals with SMS 
also have diabetes (SMS 3  and  4). 
Immunoprecipitation of GAD protein 
A total of 15 yl of diluted serum (diluted 1/10 to 1/50,000) from individ- 
uals with stiff-man syndrome, new-onset IDDM, or from control subjects 
was incubated with 30 yl of metabolically-labeled GAD protein for 12 to 
15 h at 4°C in a total assay volume of 60 pI (23). Based on percent 
incorporation rate of [3sS]methionine, 50,000 cpm of each GAD protein 
were used  in each assay tube. All dilutions of serum and GAD protein were 
made with Tris-buffered saline/0.05% Tween 20 (TBST). Protein A-Sepha- 
rose (PAS, Sigma Chemical Co., St. Louis, MO) was washed and resus- 
pended in TBST to a 2% solution. Six microliters of PAS (final  bed vol- 
ume) were added to the reaction and mixed for 1 h  at 4°C with gentle 
rotation. Using this volume of PAS, protein A is  in excess of  Ig  in the 
serum (manufacturer's specification). We confirmed experimentally that 6 
yl of PAS quantitatively immunoprecipitates Igs from the serum samples. 
The protein A-Sepharose pellets were washed three times with 500 pl of 
TBST and resuspended in 100 yl of 1% SDS and counted by p scintillation 
counting. All samples were assayed in duplicates. The relative amount of 
GAD protein immunoprecipitated was expressed as a molar ratio ((cpm of 
GAD protein immunoprecipitated by test serum minus cpm  of GAD pro- 
tein immunoprecipitated by normal serum)/(number of methionine residues 
in the GAD protein fragment)) as previously described (23). In  an inter- 
laboratory comparison of GAD Ab assays (29), this assay was positive in 
82% of sera from individuals with new-onset diabetes, 100% of bera from 
individuals with prediabetes, and 3% of normal individuals (1994 Work- 
shop results). Whether SMS or IDDM sera reacted with a particular GAD 
fragment was determined by assaying normal sera in parallel and from 
standards established during our laboratory's participation in international 
GAD Ab workshops (29, 30). A serum was determined to be positive for 
a particular GAD fragment if its reactivity exceeded the reactivity of five 
normal sera with that GAD fragment. 
Blocking of Ab  binding to GAD protein 
Unlabeled, full length GAD  65,  GAD 67, and GAD protein fragments were 
prepared in the reticulocyte lysate system as detailed above except that the 
amino acid mixture contained only unlabeled methionine. Since the me- 
thionine concentration in the reticulocyte lysate system is not limiting, 
similar amounts of cold and labeled protein were synthesized in a trans- 
lation reaction, diluted to the desired molar ratios, and then used for com- 
petition studies. For competition experiments. a dilution curve of a partic- 
ular serum was used to select the serum dilution in which binding to the 
GAD protein was easily detectable but less than maximum. Both labeled 
and unlabeled translation reactions were diluted five to eightfold so that the 
molar ratio of labeled protein to cold protein was 1 :3 to 1 :6.  The molar ratio 
was the same for different protein fragments. For the blocking studies, 
unlabeled GAD protein or reticulocyte lysate without GAD protein (neg- 
ative control) was incubated with a dilution of the test serum for 3 h at 
room temperature; this mixture was then added to 50,000 cpm of 
["SICAD protein and incubated for 12 to 15 h at 4°C (23). Each serum 
used in the blocking studies was diluted according to a previously per- 
formed serum dilution curve to allow for detection of Ab activity and to 
insure that the blocking assay was performed under the condition of Ag 
excess (serum dilutions ranged from 1/100 to 1/1000). PAS was added and 
immunoprecipitation was performed as described above. The immunopre- 
cipitate was analyzed by scintillation counting and expressed as the per- 
centage of inhibition of GAD binding following preincubation with reticu- 
locyte lysate without GAD protein. 
Synthesis of GAD peptides 
Synthetic  GAD  65  peptides  (20  amino  acids in length)  were  synthesized 
as previously  described (16) and  had a purity  greater than 85% by mass 
spectroscopy.
